current_answer: An aging clock is a model applied to a measurement. Its result can describe age resemblance, a health-related phenotype, risk or pace. Similar-looking numbers do not necessarily answer the same question.
summary: The same DNA profiles can produce a material platform offset: in the matched Hannum example reconstructed here, EPIC minus 450K averaged −1.96 years under the stated preprocessing and implementation conditions.
Calibration can remove a shared offset without proving that two platforms are interchangeable. Raw score, age gap and age-adjusted residual are different quantities and should not be mixed.

A reported before/after change becomes decision evidence only when the exact pipeline is versioned and analytical error, biological variation, construct validity and a prespecified decision threshold are all addressed.
The six-clock rentosertib analysis has a reported patient-label randomization check, but its selected 42-person cohort cannot establish aging-specific efficacy.
uncertainty: The review is selective, not a systematic census; it does not identify one true age or an overall best clock.
The documentary audit did not establish that buying a testing-and-advice package improves long-term outcomes relative to a realistic no-test alternative.
The matched-platform result is implementation-specific, not a universal correction factor; individual commercial pipeline thresholds were not established.
Some reliability results were reconstructed from reported aggregate values rather than raw participant-level data, so their stated assumptions and rounding limits remain part of the result.
The six-clock analysis uses selected participants and author-reported significance counts; its numerical supplement and permutation were not independently reproduced.
freshness_note: Foundation reviewed 21 September 2026; reliability and calibration reviewed 22 September 2026; intervention evidence reviewed 26 September 2026. A bounded documentary review, not a diagnostic or treatment service.
